informal_statement: In the context \( T \), a statement \( \varphi \) is strongly provable if and only if it is weakly provable, where strong provability (\( \vdash! \)) and weak provability (\( \vdash_2! \)) are equivalent notions within the system \( T \).
informal_proof:
To establish the equivalence between strong and weak provability in \( T \), we proceed in two directions. 

First, assume that \( \varphi \) is strongly provable (\( T \vdash! \varphi \)). By the definition of strong provability, this implies that there exists a unique proof of \( \varphi \) within \( T \). Due to the equivalency defined by the theorem `derivable_iff_derivable2`, this unique proof also qualifies as a valid weak proof, hence \( T \vdash_2.! \varphi \).

Conversely, assume \( \varphi \) is weakly provable (\( T \vdash_2.! \varphi \)). According to the `derivable_iff_derivable2` theorem, the notion of weak provability aligns with strong provability in this system. Therefore, if \( \varphi \) is weakly provable, it must also be strongly provable, establishing \( T \vdash! \varphi \).

Thus, the equivalence \( T \vdash! \varphi \leftrightarrow T \vdash_2.! \varphi \) holds in \( T \), completing the proof.

variable {L : Language} [(k : ℕ) → DecidableEq (L.Func k)] [(k : ℕ) → DecidableEq (L.Rel k)]
informal_statement: For any list of formulas Γ and a type theory T, the derivability of Γ is equivalent to the derivability of its set representation Γ.toFinset.
informal_proof:
To establish the equivalence between the derivability of a list of formulas Γ and its set representation Γ.toFinset, we will demonstrate both directions of the implication.

**First Direction (⇒):**  
Assume that Γ is T derivable!. By applying the conversion function to a derivation ending with Γ, we obtain a derivation ending with Γ.toFinset. This conversion respects the logical structure of the derivations and ensures that if Γ can be derived, so can Γ.toFinset. Therefore, if Γ is T derivable!, then Γ.toFinset is T derivable! as well.

**Second Direction (⇐):**  
Conversely, assume that Γ.toFinset is T derivable!. By reversing the previous conversion or applying the toDerivation function, we can derive Γ from Γ.toFinset. Specifically, allowing for multiple occurrences of formulas in Γ does not affect the derivability, as Γ.toFinset already accounts for the necessary logical structure. Hence, if Γ.toFinset is T derivable!, it follows that Γ is T derivable! as well.

In both directions, the conversions used preserve the essence of derivability, thereby establishing the equivalence between T derivable! Γ and T derivable! Γ.toFinset.

import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic.Calculus

# Derivation2

Different characterizations of proof.

-/

namespace LO.FirstOrder

variable {L : Language} [(k : ℕ) → DecidableEq (L.Func k)] [(k : ℕ) → DecidableEq (L.Rel k)]

section derivation2

inductive Derivation2 (T : Theory L) : Finset (SyntacticFormula L) → Type _
| closed (Δ) (φ : SyntacticFormula L)      : φ ∈ Δ → ∼φ ∈ Δ → Derivation2 T Δ

| and   {Δ} {φ ψ : SyntacticFormula L}     : φ ⋏ ψ ∈ Δ → Derivation2 T (insert φ Δ) → Derivation2 T (insert ψ Δ) → Derivation2 T Δ
| or    {Δ} {φ ψ : SyntacticFormula L}     : φ ⋎ ψ ∈ Δ → Derivation2 T (insert φ (insert ψ Δ)) → Derivation2 T Δ
| all   {Δ} {φ : SyntacticSemiformula L 1} : ∀' φ ∈ Δ → Derivation2 T (insert (Rewriting.free φ) (Δ.image Rewriting.shift)) → Derivation2 T Δ
| ex    {Δ} {φ : SyntacticSemiformula L 1} : ∃' φ ∈ Δ → (t : SyntacticTerm L) → Derivation2 T (insert (φ/[t]) Δ) → Derivation2 T Δ
| wk    {Δ Γ} : Derivation2 T Δ → Δ ⊆ Γ → Derivation2 T Γ
| shift {Δ}   : Derivation2 T Δ → Derivation2 T (Δ.image Rewriting.shift)
| cut   {Δ φ} : Derivation2 T (insert φ Δ) → Derivation2 T (insert (∼φ) Δ) → Derivation2 T Δ

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.Derivation.rewrite
rag.content:
def rewrite {Δ} : T ⟹ Δ → ∀ (f : ℕ → SyntacticTerm L), T ⟹ Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ
  | axL Δ r v,            f =>
    Derivation.cast (axL (Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ) r (fun i ↦ Rew.rewrite f (v i))) (by simp[rew_rel, rew_nrel])
  | verum Δ,              f => Derivation.cast (verum (Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ)) (by simp)
  | @or _ _ Δ φ ψ d,      f =>
    have : T ⟹ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ ⋎ Rew.rewrite f ▹ ψ :: Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ :=
      or (Derivation.cast (rewrite d f) (by simp))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @and _ _ Δ φ ψ dp dq, f =>
    have : T ⟹ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ ⋏ Rew.rewrite f ▹ ψ :: Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ :=
      and (Derivation.cast (rewrite dp f) (by simp)) (Derivation.cast (rewrite dq f) (by simp))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @all _ _ Δ φ d,       f =>
    have : T ⟹ ((Rewriting.free φ) :: Δ⁺).map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite (&0 :>ₙ fun x => Rew.shift (f x)) ▹ φ :=
      rewrite d (&0 :>ₙ fun x => Rew.shift (f x))
    have : T ⟹ (∀' Rew.rewrite (Rew.bShift ∘ f) ▹ φ) :: Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ :=
      all (Derivation.cast this (by simp [free_rewrite_eq, Rewriting.shifts, shift_rewrite_eq, Finset.image_image, Function.comp_def]))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp[Rew.q_rewrite])
  | @ex _ _ Δ φ t d,      f =>
    have : T ⟹ (φ/[t] :: Δ).map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ := rewrite d f
    have : T ⟹ (∃' Rew.rewrite (Rew.bShift ∘ f) ▹ φ) :: Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ :=

    have dΓ : T ⟹ ∼(Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ) :: Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ := Derivation.cast (rewrite dn f) (by simp)

rag.content:
protected unsafe def repr {Δ : Sequent L} : T ⟹ Δ → String
  | axL Δ _ _   =>
      "\\AxiomC{}\n" ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize(axL)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr Δ ++ "$}\n\n"
  | verum Δ       =>
      "\\AxiomC{}\n" ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize($\\top$)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr Δ ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @or _ _ Δ φ ψ d      =>
      Derivation.repr d ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize($\\lor$)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr ((φ ⋎ ψ) :: Δ) ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @and _ _ Δ φ ψ dp dq =>
      Derivation.repr dp ++
      Derivation.repr dq ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize($\\land$)}\n" ++
      "\\BinaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr ((φ ⋏ ψ) :: Δ) ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @all _ _ Δ φ d       =>
      Derivation.repr d ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize($\\forall$)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr ((∀' φ) :: Δ) ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @ex _ _ Δ φ _ d      =>
      Derivation.repr d ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize($\\exists$)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr ((∃' φ) :: Δ) ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @wk _ _ _ Γ d _      =>
      Derivation.repr d ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize(wk)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr Γ ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @cut _ _ Δ _ dp dn =>
      Derivation.repr dp ++
      Derivation.repr dn ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize(Cut)}\n" ++
      "\\BinaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr Δ ++ "$}\n\n"
  | root (φ := φ) _   =>
      "\\AxiomC{}\n" ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize(ROOT)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr φ ++ ", " ++ reprStr (∼φ) ++ "$}\n\n"

rag.content:
def lMap (Φ : L₁ →ᵥ L₂) {Δ} : T₁ ⟹ Δ → T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ Δ.map (.lMap Φ)
  | axL Δ r v            =>
    .cast (axL (Δ.map (.lMap Φ)) (Φ.rel r) (fun i ↦ .lMap Φ (v i)))
    (by simp [Semiformula.lMap_rel, Semiformula.lMap_nrel])
  | verum Δ              => by simpa using verum _
  | @or _ _ Δ φ ψ d      => by
    have : T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ (.lMap Φ φ ⋎ .lMap Φ ψ :: Δ.map (.lMap Φ) : Sequent L₂) :=
      or (by simpa using lMap Φ d)
    exact Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @and _ _ Δ φ ψ dp dq =>
    have : T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ (.lMap Φ φ ⋏ .lMap Φ ψ :: (Δ.map (.lMap Φ)) : Sequent L₂) :=
      and (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ dp) (by simp)) (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ dq) (by simp))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @all _ _ Δ φ d       =>
    have : T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ ((∀' .lMap Φ φ) :: (Δ.map (.lMap Φ)) : Sequent L₂) :=
      all (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ d) (by simp[←Semiformula.lMap_free, shifts_image]))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @ex _ _ Δ φ t d      =>
    have : T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ ((∃' .lMap Φ φ) :: (Δ.map (.lMap Φ)) : Sequent L₂) :=
      ex (Semiterm.lMap Φ t)
        (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ d) (by simp[Semiformula.lMap_substs, Matrix.constant_eq_singleton]))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @wk _ _ Δ Γ d ss     => (lMap Φ d).wk (List.map_subset _ ss)
  | @cut _ _ Δ φ d dn    =>
    have : T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ (Δ.map (.lMap Φ) : Sequent L₂) :=
      cut (φ := .lMap Φ φ) (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ d) (by simp)) (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ dn) (by simp))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp[Finset.image_union])
  | root h               => root (Set.mem_image_of_mem _ h)

informal_statement: The function `Derivation.toDerivation2` transforms a given derivation `d` into another derivation `d'` by applying context-preserving operations that handle various logical connectives and structural rules, ensuring that the resulting derivation adheres to the specified logical framework.
informal_proof:
The function `Derivation.toDerivation2` processes the given derivation `d` by applying a series of context-preserving operations:

1. **Axiom Case (`Derivation.axL`):** The function constructs a derivation `d'` by simplifying the context, ensuring that the axiom rules are correctly handled.

2. **Root Case (`Derivation.root`):** A direct derivation is returned without any transformation, preserving the root structure.

3. **True Case (`Derivation.verum`):** The function trivially returns a closed derivation, confirming the verum proposition's validity.

4. **Conjunction Cases (`Derivation.and`, `Derivation.or`):** For conjunctions, the function splits the derivation into components, transforming each side appropriately while maintaining the context through `simp` simplifications.

5. **Quantifiers (`Derivation.all`, `Derivation.ex`):** The function applies the same transformations to quantified expressions, ensuring variable context is maintained.

6. **Weakening (`Derivation.wk`):** An additional context assumption is added, preserving the existing derivation's validity under the expanded context.

7. **Cut Rule (`Derivation.cut`):** The function combines two derivations by aligning their respective contexts and ensuring the cut rule is appropriately addressed.

By methodically addressing each rule and structural aspect, `Derivation.toDerivation2` ensures a coherent and logically consistent transformation of the input derivation into the desired output.

rag.name: Equiv.Perm.map_finRange_perm
rag.content:
theorem Equiv.Perm.map_finRange_perm {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) :
    map σ (finRange n) ~ finRange n := by
  rw [perm_ext_iff_of_nodup ((nodup_finRange n).map σ.injective) <| nodup_finRange n]
  simpa [mem_map, mem_finRange] using σ.surjective

informal_statement: Applying a shift operation to a Sequent Δ and then converting it to a Finset is equivalent to converting Δ to a Finset and then shifting each element of the resulting set.
informal_proof: To establish the equivalence, we proceed by extensionality, considering an arbitrary element φ. By applying the definition of the shifting operation, we demonstrate that φ belongs to the Finset obtained by shifting Δ if and only if it belongs to the image of Δ's Finset under shifting. This involves showing that the application of the shift operation is consistent with the conversion to a Finset in both directions, thereby confirming the equality of the two resulting sets.

informal_statement: The formula φ is derivable from the theory T under conditions that involve exactly one premise or exactly one derivation step.
informal_proof:
To show that φ is derivable from theory T under the condition of having exactly one premise or exactly one derivation step, we proceed as follows:

1. **Understanding the Notation**: The notation "T ⊢₂! {φ}" signifies that φ is derivable from theory T with the specification that there is exactly one premise involved in the derivation. The subscript 2! likely indicates that the derivation rule or process involves two specific conditions or steps, one of which is critical to the uniqueness.

2. **Derivation Conditions**: By definition, a derivation from T means that we start with axioms or assumptions within T and apply valid inference rules to arrive at φ. The condition "₂!" suggests that there is a precise mechanism ensuring that only one of the two considered possibilities leads to φ being derivable.

3. **Uniqueness of Derivation**: The subscript exclamation mark emphasizes the uniqueness aspect of the derivation. Within the framework of T, only one specific path or application of an inference rule leads to φ, thereby precluding other derivations that might not satisfy the same stringent conditions.

4. **Conclusion**: Therefore, φ is uniquely derivable from T via a process that adheres to exactly one derivation pathway, as specified by the "₂!" notation.

variable {L : Language} [(k : ℕ) → DecidableEq (L.Func k)] [(k : ℕ) → DecidableEq (L.Rel k)]
informal_statement: The OR operator in Boolean algebra is associative. This means that for any propositions \( \phi \), \( \psi \), and \( \chi \), the expression \( \phi \lor (\psi \lor \chi) \) is logically equivalent to \( (\phi \lor \psi) \lor \chi \).
informal_proof:
To prove the associativity of the OR operator, we proceed as follows:

1. **Assumption**: By definition, we start with the expressions \( \phi \lor (\psi \lor \chi) \) and \( (\phi \lor \psi) \lor \chi \).

2. **Distributive Law**: We use the known properties of logical OR, including commutativity \( (A \lor B) = (B \lor A) \) and idempotence \( (A \lor A) = A \), to manipulate the expressions.

3. **Associativity Demonstration**: 
    - Apply associativity to the first expression:
      \[
      \phi \lor (\psi \lor \chi) \equiv (\phi \lor \psi) \lor \chi
      \]
    - By applying the same associativity axiom, we directly obtain the equivalence.

4. **Conclusion**: Therefore, any number of OR operations can be grouped in any order without changing the truth value of the expression, establishing the associativity of OR.

<PROOF>
To align with the Cut Rule in sequent calculus, we observe that in classical logic, any formula \( \phi \) or its negation \( \neg\phi \) holds within the system. If \( \Delta \) combines with either \( \phi \) or its negation and still leads to a valid derivation, it implies that the truth of \( \phi \)'s negation doesn't interfere with the ability to derive \( \Delta \). C1_dependencies.compilationAlias: abbrev Theory (L : Language) := Set (SyntacticFormula L)

C0_dependencies.name: LO.FirstOrder.Derivation2.brecOn
C0_dependencies.content:
inductive Derivation2 (T : Theory L) : Finset (SyntacticFormula L) → Type _
| closed (Δ) (φ : SyntacticFormula L)      : φ ∈ Δ → ∼φ ∈ Δ → Derivation2 T Δ
| root  {Δ} (φ : SyntacticFormula L)       : φ ∈ T → φ ∈ Δ → Derivation2 T Δ
| verum {Δ}                                : ⊤ ∈ Δ → Derivation2 T Δ
| and   {Δ} {φ ψ : SyntacticFormula L}     : φ ⋏ ψ ∈ Δ → Derivation2 T (insert φ Δ) → Derivation2 T (insert ψ Δ) → Derivation2 T Δ
| or    {Δ} {φ ψ : SyntacticFormula L}     : φ ⋎ ψ ∈ Δ → Derivation2 T (insert φ (insert ψ Δ)) → Derivation2 T Δ
| all   {Δ} {φ : SyntacticSemiformula L 1} : ∀' φ ∈ Δ → Derivation2 T (insert (Rewriting.free φ) (Δ.image Rewriting.shift)) → Derivation2 T Δ
| ex    {Δ} {φ : SyntacticSemiformula L 1} : ∃' φ ∈ Δ → (t : SyntacticTerm L) → Derivation2 T (insert (φ/[t]) Δ) → Derivation2 T Δ
| wk    {Δ Γ} : Derivation2 T Δ → Δ ⊆ Γ → Derivation2 T Γ
| shift {Δ}   : Derivation2 T Δ → Derivation2 T (Δ.image Rewriting.shift)
| cut   {Δ φ} : Derivation2 T (insert φ Δ) → Derivation2 T (insert (∼φ) Δ) → Derivation2 T Δ

def specialize {φ : SyntacticSemiformula L 1} (t : SyntacticTerm L) :
    T ⟹ (∀' φ) :: Γ → T ⟹ φ/[t] :: Γ := fun d ↦
  have : T ⟹ ∼φ/[t] :: φ/[t] :: Γ := Tait.em (φ := φ/[t]) (by simp) (by simp)
  have dn : T ⟹ ∼(∀' φ) :: φ/[t] :: Γ := by
    simp only [neg_all, Nat.reduceAdd, Nat.succ_eq_add_one]
    exact Derivation.ex t (by simpa using this)
  have dp : T ⟹ (∀' φ) :: φ/[t] :: Γ :=
    Derivation.wk d (List.cons_subset_cons _ <| by simp)
  Derivation.cut dp dn

variable {L : Language} [(k : ℕ) → DecidableEq (L.Func k)] [(k : ℕ) → DecidableEq (L.Rel k)]
informal_statement: In a type theory system, given any context Δ and a term t in Δ, there exists a way to insert a formula φ at the position of t such that the resulting context Δ' still allows for a derivation of the same type as Δ.
informal_proof:
First, we fix a context Δ and a term t in Δ.

Since φ is in Δ, we can perform a substitution where φ is inserted in place of t.

After substitution, the resulting context Δ' will still be admissible in the type theory system.

Therefore, the derivation can be adjusted to accommodate the inserted formula φ while maintaining the type-theoretic validity.

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.Derivation.repr
rag.content:
protected unsafe def repr {Δ : Sequent L} : T ⟹ Δ → String
  | axL Δ _ _   =>
      "\\AxiomC{}\n" ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize(axL)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr Δ ++ "$}\n\n"
  | verum Δ       =>
      "\\AxiomC{}\n" ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize($\\top$)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr Δ ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @or _ _ Δ φ ψ d      =>
      Derivation.repr d ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize($\\lor$)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr ((φ ⋎ ψ) :: Δ) ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @and _ _ Δ φ ψ dp dq =>
      Derivation.repr dp ++
      Derivation.repr dq ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize($\\land$)}\n" ++
      "\\BinaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr ((φ ⋏ ψ) :: Δ) ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @all _ _ Δ φ d       =>
      Derivation.repr d ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize($\\forall$)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr ((∀' φ) :: Δ) ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @ex _ _ Δ φ _ d      =>
      Derivation.repr d ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize($\\exists$)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr ((∃' φ) :: Δ) ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @wk _ _ _ Γ d _      =>
      Derivation.repr d ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize(wk)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr Γ ++ "$}\n\n"
  | @cut _ _ Δ _ dp dn =>
      Derivation.repr dp ++
      Derivation.repr dn ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize(Cut)}\n" ++
      "\\BinaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr Δ ++ "$}\n\n"
  | root (φ := φ) _   =>
      "\\AxiomC{}\n" ++
      "\\RightLabel{\\scriptsize(ROOT)}\n" ++
      "\\UnaryInfC{$" ++ reprStr φ ++ ", " ++ reprStr (∼φ) ++ "$}\n\n"

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.Derivation.rewrite
rag.content:
def rewrite {Δ} : T ⟹ Δ → ∀ (f : ℕ → SyntacticTerm L), T ⟹ Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ
  | axL Δ r v,            f =>
    Derivation.cast (axL (Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ) r (fun i ↦ Rew.rewrite f (v i))) (by simp[rew_rel, rew_nrel])
  | verum Δ,              f => Derivation.cast (verum (Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ)) (by simp)
  | @or _ _ Δ φ ψ d,      f =>
    have : T ⟹ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ ⋎ Rew.rewrite f ▹ ψ :: Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ :=
      or (Derivation.cast (rewrite d f) (by simp))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @and _ _ Δ φ ψ dp dq, f =>
    have : T ⟹ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ ⋏ Rew.rewrite f ▹ ψ :: Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ :=
      and (Derivation.cast (rewrite dp f) (by simp)) (Derivation.cast (rewrite dq f) (by simp))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @all _ _ Δ φ d,       f =>
    have : T ⟹ ((Rewriting.free φ) :: Δ⁺).map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite (&0 :>ₙ fun x => Rew.shift (f x)) ▹ φ :=
      rewrite d (&0 :>ₙ fun x => Rew.shift (f x))
    have : T ⟹ (∀' Rew.rewrite (Rew.bShift ∘ f) ▹ φ) :: Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ :=
      all (Derivation.cast this (by simp [free_rewrite_eq, Rewriting.shifts, shift_rewrite_eq, Finset.image_image, Function.comp_def]))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp[Rew.q_rewrite])
  | @ex _ _ Δ φ t d,      f =>
    have : T ⟹ (φ/[t] :: Δ).map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ := rewrite d f
    have : T ⟹ (∃' Rew.rewrite (Rew.bShift ∘ f) ▹ φ) :: Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ :=
      ex (Rew.rewrite f t) (Derivation.cast this (by simp[rewrite_subst_eq]))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp[Rew.q_rewrite])
  | @wk _ _ Δ Γ d ss,     f => (rewrite d f).wk (List.map_subset _ ss)
  | @cut _ _ Δ φ d dn,    f =>
    have dΔ : T ⟹ (Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ) :: Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ := Derivation.cast (rewrite d f) (by simp)
    have dΓ : T ⟹ ∼(Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ) :: Δ.map fun φ ↦ Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ := Derivation.cast (rewrite dn f) (by simp)
    Derivation.cast (cut dΔ dΓ) (by simp)
  | root h,               f => rewrite₁ (root h) f

rag.content:
def trans (F : U ⊢* T) {Γ : Sequent L} : T ⟹ Γ → U ⟹ Γ
  | axL Γ R v => axL Γ R v
  | verum Γ   => verum Γ
  | and d₁ d₂ => and (trans F d₁) (trans F d₂)
  | or d      => or (trans F d)
  | all d     => all (trans F d)
  | ex t d    => ex t (trans F d)
  | wk d ss   => wk (trans F d) ss
  | cut d₁ d₂ => cut (trans F d₁) (trans F d₂)
  | root h    => F h

rag.content:
private def deductionAux {Γ : Sequent L} : T ⟹ Γ → T \ {φ} ⟹ ∼(∀∀φ) :: Γ
  | axL Γ R v       => Tait.wkTail <| axL Γ R v
  | verum Γ         => Tait.wkTail <| verum Γ
  | and d₁ d₂       => Tait.rotate₁ <| and (Tait.rotate₁ (deductionAux d₁)) (Tait.rotate₁ (deductionAux d₂))
  | or d            => Tait.rotate₁ <| or (Tait.rotate₂ (deductionAux d))
  | all d           => Tait.rotate₁ <| all (Derivation.cast (Tait.rotate₁ (deductionAux d)) (by simp))
  | ex t d          => Tait.rotate₁ <| ex t <| Tait.rotate₁ (deductionAux d)
  | wk d ss         => wk (deductionAux d) (by simp [List.subset_cons_of_subset _ ss])
  | cut d₁ d₂       => (Tait.rotate₁ <| deductionAux d₁).cut (Tait.rotate₁ <| deductionAux d₂)
  | root (φ := ψ) h => if hq : φ = ψ then Derivation.cast (not_close' φ) (by simp [hq]) else
    have : T \ {φ} ⟹. ψ := root (by simp [h, Ne.symm hq])
    wk this (by simp)

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.Derivation.lMap
rag.content:
def lMap (Φ : L₁ →ᵥ L₂) {Δ} : T₁ ⟹ Δ → T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ Δ.map (.lMap Φ)
  | axL Δ r v            =>
    .cast (axL (Δ.map (.lMap Φ)) (Φ.rel r) (fun i ↦ .lMap Φ (v i)))
    (by simp [Semiformula.lMap_rel, Semiformula.lMap_nrel])
  | verum Δ              => by simpa using verum _
  | @or _ _ Δ φ ψ d      => by
    have : T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ (.lMap Φ φ ⋎ .lMap Φ ψ :: Δ.map (.lMap Φ) : Sequent L₂) :=
      or (by simpa using lMap Φ d)
    exact Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @and _ _ Δ φ ψ dp dq =>
    have : T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ (.lMap Φ φ ⋏ .lMap Φ ψ :: (Δ.map (.lMap Φ)) : Sequent L₂) :=
      and (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ dp) (by simp)) (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ dq) (by simp))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @all _ _ Δ φ d       =>
    have : T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ ((∀' .lMap Φ φ) :: (Δ.map (.lMap Φ)) : Sequent L₂) :=
      all (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ d) (by simp[←Semiformula.lMap_free, shifts_image]))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @ex _ _ Δ φ t d      =>
    have : T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ ((∃' .lMap Φ φ) :: (Δ.map (.lMap Φ)) : Sequent L₂) :=
      ex (Semiterm.lMap Φ t)
        (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ d) (by simp[Semiformula.lMap_substs, Matrix.constant_eq_singleton]))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp)
  | @wk _ _ Δ Γ d ss     => (lMap Φ d).wk (List.map_subset _ ss)
  | @cut _ _ Δ φ d dn    =>
    have : T₁.lMap Φ ⟹ (Δ.map (.lMap Φ) : Sequent L₂) :=
      cut (φ := .lMap Φ φ) (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ d) (by simp)) (Derivation.cast (lMap Φ dn) (by simp))
    Derivation.cast this (by simp[Finset.image_union])
  | root h               => root (Set.mem_image_of_mem _ h)

informal_statement: For every natural number \( n \), there exists a prime number \( p \) such that \( p > n \). Equivalently, there are infinitely many primes.
informal_proof:
First, consider any natural number \( n \). We analyze the number \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), where \( ! \) denotes the factorial operation. Since \( n \) is a natural number, \( n + 1 \) is at least 2, making \( (n + 1)! \) at least 2. Consequently, \( (n + 1)! + 1 \) is at least 3 and therefore has a prime factor \( p \), based on the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.

Next, we assume for the sake of contradiction that this prime factor \( p \) is not greater than \( n \), i.e., \( p \le n \). Since \( p \) is a prime number, it must divide \( (n + 1)! \), as \( p \) is one of the factors in the product that forms \( (n + 1)! \).

Given that \( p \) divides both \( (n + 1)! \) and \( (n + 1)! + 1 \), it must also divide their difference:
\[
((n + 1)! + 1) - (n + 1)! = 1
\]
This implies that \( p \) divides 1. However, the only positive integer that divides 1 is 1 itself, which contradicts the definition of \( p \) being a prime number (since primes are greater than 1). This contradiction establishes that our initial assumption is false, thereby proving that \( p \) must be greater than \( n \).

Thus, for every natural number \( n \), there exists a prime number \( p \) such that \( p > n \), demonstrating that there are infinitely many prime numbers.

informal_statement: If a set Δ contains both a formula φ and its negation ∼φ, then we can derive T from Δ.
informal_proof:
First, we assume that Δ is a set containing both a formula φ and its negation ∼φ within a logical system.

Given this assumption, we can apply the rules of the logical system to derive certain consequences. Specifically, having both φ and ∼φ in Δ is a contradiction. In most logical systems, a contradiction allows the derivation of any formula, a principle known as explosion or ex falso quodlibet.

Thus, from the contradiction of φ and ∼φ coexisting in Δ, we can derive T, which represents the consequence that follows from this contradiction.

Therefore, if Δ contains both φ and ∼φ, then T can be derived from Δ.

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.LawfulSyntacticRewriting.shift_rewrite_eq
rag.content:
lemma shift_rewrite_eq (f : ℕ → SyntacticTerm L) (φ : S 0) :
    shift (Rew.rewrite f ▹ φ) = (Rew.rewrite (&0 :>ₙ fun x ↦ Rew.shift (f x))) ▹ shift φ := by
  simpa [←comp_app] using smul_ext' <| by ext x <;> simp [Rew.comp_app]

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.Rewriting.shift
rag.content: abbrev shift [Rewriting L ℕ F ℕ F] (φ : F n) : F n := @Rew.shift L n ▹ φ

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.Derivation.genelalizeByNewver
rag.content:
def genelalizeByNewver {φ : SyntacticSemiformula L 1} (hp : ¬φ.FVar? m) (hΔ : ∀ ψ ∈ Δ, ¬ψ.FVar? m)
    (d : T ⟹ φ/[&m] :: Δ) : T ⟹ (∀' φ) :: Δ := by
  have : T ⟹ (Rewriting.free φ) :: Δ⁺ :=
    Derivation.cast (Derivation.map d (fun x => if x = m then 0 else x + 1))
    (by simp[map_subst_eq_free φ hp, map_rewriteMap_eq_shifts Δ hΔ])
  exact all this

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.Rew.emb_comp_bShift_comm
rag.content:
lemma emb_comp_bShift_comm {o : Type v₁} [IsEmpty o] :
    Rew.bShift.comp (Rew.emb : Rew L o n ξ n) = Rew.emb.comp Rew.bShift := by
  ext x; simp [comp_app]
  exact IsEmpty.elim (by assumption) x

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.Rew.emb_bShift_term
rag.content:
lemma emb_bShift_term {o : Type v₁} [IsEmpty o] (t : Semiterm L o n) :
    Rew.bShift (Rew.emb t : Semiterm L ξ n) = Rew.emb (Rew.bShift t) := by
  simp [←comp_app, emb_comp_bShift_comm]

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.Rew.q
rag.content:
protected def q (ω : Rew L ξ₁ n₁ ξ₂ n₂) : Rew L ξ₁ (n₁ + 1) ξ₂ (n₂ + 1) :=
  bind (#0 :> bShift ∘ ω ∘ bvar) (bShift ∘ ω ∘ fvar)

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.LawfulSyntacticRewriting.shiftEmb_def
rag.content:
lemma shiftEmb_def (φ : S n) :
  shiftEmb φ = shift φ := rfl

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.Derivation.shift
rag.content:
protected def shift {Δ : Sequent L} (d : T ⟹ Δ) : T ⟹ Δ⁺ :=
  Derivation.cast (Derivation.map d Nat.succ) (by simp only [Rewriting.shifts, List.map_inj_left]; intro _ _; rfl)

rag.name: LO.FirstOrder.LawfulSyntacticRewriting.free_rewrite_eq
rag.content:
lemma free_rewrite_eq (f : ℕ → SyntacticTerm L) (φ : S 1) :
    free ((Rew.rewrite fun x ↦ Rew.bShift (f x)) ▹ φ) =
    Rew.rewrite (&0 :>ₙ fun x ↦ Rew.shift (f x)) ▹ free φ := by
  simpa [← comp_app] using smul_ext' <| by ext x <;> simp [Rew.comp_app, Fin.eq_zero]

informal_statement:
Given a context of derivations in a logical system parameterized by `T`, if `Δ` is a subset of `Γ`, then any derivation from `Δ` can also be used as a derivation from `Γ`. 

In other words, weakening allows us to add additional formulas to the context without affecting the validity of existing derivations.
informal_proof:
First, we consider a derivation from `Δ`. 
Since `Δ` is a subset of `Γ`, every formula in `Δ` is also in `Γ`. 
Therefore, all the assumptions used in the original derivation are included within `Γ`. 
As a result, the original derivation can be directly applied to `Γ`, concluding the proof that a derivation from `Γ` exists.

This aligns with the idea that weakening involves introducing additional premises without changing the conclusions, thereby allowing any existing derivation from `Δ` to also be valid from `Γ` due to the subset relation.
